questions.stem: During a quarterly technology briefing at a regional retail bank, the Chief Operating Officer asks how four proposed initiatives relate to each other: (1) a static if-then compliance alert engine, (2) a gradient-boosted model scoring credit-card churn probability, (3) a convolutional neural network inspecting scanned check signatures, and (4) a system drafting personalized wealth-advisory summaries. Which statement accurately explains the hierarchical relationship among AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Generative AI to guide the board's investment taxonomy?
options: Generative AI is the broadest umbrella discipline that encompasses classical Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and static rule-based expert systems.

Artificial Intelligence is the broadest field, Machine Learning is a subset of AI that learns patterns from data, Deep Learning is a neural-network subset of ML, and Generative AI is a subset of Deep Learning capable of creating new content.
Machine Learning and Generative AI are mutually exclusive branches of computer science because Generative AI relies solely on deterministic rules rather than statistical training data.
Deep Learning is a specialized subset of Generative AI used only when organizations need structured tabular predictions rather than unstructured text or imagery.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because the standard technical hierarchy nests from broadest to most specialized: Artificial Intelligence (including rule-based systems) -> Machine Learning (learning from data, such as churn scoring) -> Deep Learning (multi-layered neural networks, such as check signature vision models) -> Generative AI (deep neural foundation models that synthesize novel text, images, audio, code, or video). Option A inverts the hierarchy by placing Generative AI above AI and classical ML. Option C is wrong because Generative AI is trained statistically on massive datasets via deep learning, not static rules. Option D reverses the Deep Learning / Generative AI nesting and misstates Deep Learning's primary strengths.
questions.use_case: Enterprise AI governance boards at financial institutions map portfolio proposals across the AI -> ML -> DL -> GenAI hierarchy so teams match classical ML (BigQuery ML / Vertex AI Tabular) to numerical forecasting and Gemini foundation models to content synthesis.
questions.hack: Russian nesting dolls rule: AI (broadest) > Machine Learning (learns from data) > Deep Learning (multi-layer neural nets) > Generative AI (creates new content).

questions.domain: Domain 2: Google Cloud's Generative AI Offerings
questions.stem: A product innovation squad at a multinational insurance carrier built a working claims-triage prototype in two days using Gemini models inside Google AI Studio with a personal developer API key. Before launching the assistant to 4,500 licensed adjusters handling regulated policyholder records, the Chief Information Security Officer requires IAM role-based access control, VPC Service Controls data-exfiltration perimeters, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and enterprise SLAs. What should the engineering director recommend?
options: Continue running production traffic in Google AI Studio and rotate the shared API key every 24 hours via a cron job.
Export the prototype prompts into a consumer Gemini web workspace and assign each adjuster an individual Gmail login.
Migrate the Gemini workload from Google AI Studio to Vertex AI inside a governed Google Cloud project to gain IAM, VPC Service Controls, CMEK, and enterprise compliance guarantees.
Replace Gemini with a self-built rule engine because Google Cloud does not support VPC Service Controls or CMEK for foundation models.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Google AI Studio is designed for rapid individual developer prototyping with lightweight API keys, whereas Vertex AI is Google Cloud's unified enterprise AI platform providing granular Cloud IAM, VPC Service Controls, CMEK, regional data residency, audit logging, and production SLAs. Option A fails because rotating API keys in AI Studio does not provide VPC-SC perimeters, CMEK, or enterprise governance. Option B violates enterprise security and privacy policies by routing regulated policyholder data through consumer accounts. Option D is factually false because Vertex AI natively supports VPC-SC, CMEK, and zero-data-training enterprise commitments.
questions.use_case: Enterprise digital teams rapidly iterate prompts and multimodal tests in Google AI Studio, then click 'Get Code' to deploy the production pipeline onto Vertex AI endpoints governed by organization-wide IAM, Cloud KMS CMEK, and VPC Service Controls.
questions.hack: Google AI Studio = fast developer prototyping with API keys; Vertex AI = production enterprise scale with IAM, VPC-SC, CMEK, and SLAs.

questions.domain: Domain 3: Techniques to Improve Generative AI Model Output
questions.stem: A corporate legal operations team uses a Gemini model on Vertex AI to classify incoming vendor indemnification clauses into four internal risk tiers: TIER_1_AUTO_APPROVE, TIER_2_STANDARD_REDLINE, TIER_3_COUNSEL_REVIEW, and TIER_4_ESCALATE_GC. With a plain instruction naming the four labels, the model classifies obvious clauses well but inconsistently interprets subtle liability caps and occasionally invents extra label names. The team wants the fastest, lowest-cost way to improve classification consistency without training a custom model. What technique should they apply first?
options: Add few-shot prompting by supplying 4 to 6 representative clause-and-tier examples inside the prompt to demonstrate boundary cases and exact output labels.
Collect 50,000 labeled clauses and launch full supervised fine-tuning of a new base model before modifying the prompt.
Raise the sampling temperature to 1.6 so the model explores broader legal interpretations for every clause.
Switch from a text LLM to an Imagen diffusion model because image models enforce stricter classification taxonomies.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because few-shot prompting embeds a small set of high-signal input/output examples directly in the prompt, anchoring both nuanced decision boundaries and exact label syntax at zero training cost and minimal latency overhead. Option B violates the GenAI adaptation hierarchy by jumping to expensive full fine-tuning before exhausting prompt engineering. Option C increases randomness and worsens label inconsistency instead of stabilizing classification. Option D is nonsensical because Imagen generates and edits images rather than classifying legal text.
questions.use_case: Legal, procurement, and compliance teams place 3 to 8 edge-case examples inside a Vertex AI prompt template (paired with structured output) to standardize clause triage before considering PEFT/LoRA adaptation.
questions.hack: Zero-shot drifts on subtle edge cases or formatting -> upgrade to Few-Shot Prompting (3-6 concrete input/output examples) first.

questions.domain: Domain 4: Business Strategies for Successful GenAI Solutions
questions.stem: Over the past nine months, enthusiastic engineers across a global industrial manufacturer built more than 35 Generative AI prototypes during internal hackathons. Despite strong technical demos, not a single prototype has reached production because business unit presidents lack shared priorities, security approvals stall indefinitely, and no funding exists to operationalize pilots. Which organizational transformation pattern best resolves this 'pilot purgatory'?
options: Shut down all grassroots employee experimentation permanently and outsource every future AI idea to external agencies.
Allow each factory manager to purchase separate unapproved consumer AI subscriptions using corporate travel cards.
Mandate that every engineering team pre-train its own proprietary foundation model from scratch before presenting to leadership.
Combine top-down executive sponsorship (aligned strategic goals, budget, and governance guardrails) with structured bottom-up team experimentation.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Google Cloud's GenAI executive transformation playbook emphasizes pairing top-down executive sponsorship (clear business priorities, funding, security/governance pathways) with bottom-up experimentation (empowering frontline builders to surface real pain points) so winning pilots smoothly graduate into production. Option A kills frontline innovation and institutional learning. Option B creates shadow AI, data leakage, and compliance exposure. Option C wastes millions of dollars and years of effort without solving governance or executive alignment.
questions.use_case: Global enterprises pair an executive AI steering committee (setting ROI gates and fast-track security reviews) with bottom-up Vertex AI sandbox programs so promising prototypes graduate into funded production products.
questions.hack: Stuck in hackathon/pilot purgatory = missing Top-Down Executive Sponsorship paired with Bottom-Up Experimentation.

questions.stem: A healthcare logistics company is establishing a standardized Machine Learning lifecycle for its analytics and AI teams to move models reliably from raw operational records to sustained production value. Which sequence represents the proper end-to-end ML lifecycle order?
options: Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Deploy model endpoint to production -> (2) Ingest and clean raw operational data -> (3) Train and evaluate candidate models -> (4) Define business objective and feature definitions.

Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Ingest, clean, and prepare high-quality data with feature engineering -> (2) Train and tune candidate models on training splits -> (3) Evaluate accuracy, fairness, and business metrics on held-out test sets -> (4) Deploy to production and continuously monitor for data drift and performance decay.
Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Monitor production drift -> (2) Evaluate test accuracy -> (3) Clean raw training datasets -> (4) Train production model without validation.

Order 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4: (1) Train deep learning models on uncleaned raw logs -> (2) Deploy directly to customers -> (3) Perform feature engineering after deployment -> (4) Ingest source data retroactively.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because a disciplined ML lifecycle progresses sequentially from (1) data ingestion, cleaning, preparation, and feature engineering -> (2) model training/tuning -> (3) rigorous offline evaluation on held-out test datasets for quality and fairness -> (4) production deployment paired with ongoing drift and performance monitoring. Options A, C, and D scramble mandatory dependencies by deploying or monitoring before data preparation, training, and evaluation occur.
questions.use_case: Organizations orchestrate this exact lifecycle end-to-end in Vertex AI Pipelines, Vertex AI Model Registry, Vertex AI Evaluation, and Vertex AI Model Monitoring to prevent silent accuracy decay after go-live.
questions.hack: ML Lifecycle Golden Sequence: Data Prep/Features -> Train -> Evaluate -> Deploy & Monitor Drift.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Google Cloud's Generative AI Offerings
questions.stem: An investment-banking advisory practice wants to build an internal deal-diligence workbench on Vertex AI that reads 800-page financial disclosures, cross-checks complex accounting footnotes against acquisition agreements, synthesizes multi-step valuation risks, and writes Python sensitivity models. Latency of several seconds per query is acceptable, but maximum analytical reasoning depth and multimodal accuracy are non-negotiable. Which Google model family tier best fits this workload?
options: Gemini Pro, engineered for complex multi-step reasoning, deep coding, and long-context multimodal analysis.
Gemini Flash-Lite, optimized exclusively for ultra-low-cost, shallow high-volume classification tasks.
Chirp, Google Cloud's universal speech-recognition model for multilingual audio transcription.
Imagen, Google Cloud's diffusion model for photorealistic enterprise image generation and editing.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because Gemini Pro is Google's flagship reasoning tier designed for complex analytical synthesis, long-context multimodal document comprehension, nuanced financial/legal reasoning, and sophisticated code generation. Option B (Gemini Flash-Lite) trades maximum reasoning depth for ultra-low latency and minimal per-token cost in high-throughput workloads. Option C (Chirp) specializes in speech-to-text transcription rather than document analysis or Python coding. Option D (Imagen) generates and edits visual imagery rather than performing textual/numerical diligence.
questions.use_case: M&A teams, enterprise architects, and R&D groups route complex multi-document diligence, legal synthesis, and intricate codebase debugging to Gemini Pro on Vertex AI while offloading simple routing tasks to Gemini Flash.
questions.hack: Complex multi-step reasoning + deep coding + nuanced long-context analysis (latency tolerant) = Gemini Pro.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Google Cloud's Generative AI Offerings
questions.stem: The General Counsel of a pharmaceutical manufacturer halts a proposed Vertex AI clinical-trial summarization project, warning that submitting confidential Phase III trial protocols to Gemini will cause Google to absorb proprietary drug formulas into public foundation models accessible by competitors. Which official Google Cloud commitment directly addresses this concern?
options: Google Cloud trains its public Gemini models on customer Vertex AI prompts only after waiting 90 days.
Google Cloud requires customers to purchase dedicated Cloud TPU pods before prompt privacy protections apply.
Google Cloud shares Vertex AI prompt logs across enterprise tenants in the same industry to improve domain benchmarks.

Google Cloud's enterprise privacy commitment guarantees that customer prompts, grounding data, and fine-tuning datasets processed on Vertex AI are never used to train Google's shared foundation models without explicit customer permission.
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Google Cloud explicitly commits under its Cloud Data Processing Addendum and Vertex AI enterprise privacy governance that customer inputs, outputs, grounding corpora, and tuned adapter weights remain strictly owned by the customer and are never used to train Google's public or shared foundation models. Options A and C directly contradict Google Cloud's zero-data-training guarantee. Option B is false because enterprise data privacy applies by default across pay-as-you-go Vertex AI APIs as well as Provisioned Throughput.
questions.use_case: Regulated pharma, banking, and defense organizations cite Google Cloud's contractual Zero-Data-Training commitment (paired with Zero Data Retention options and CMEK) during BISO and legal sign-off reviews.
questions.hack: Enterprise customer data in Vertex AI is YOUR data: Google NEVER uses it to train shared foundation models.

questions.stem: A consumer lending institution is deploying two AI capabilities simultaneously: System X predicts the exact probability (between 0.0 and 1.0) that a mortgage applicant will default within 24 months based on credit bureau features, while System Y drafts customized, empathetic payment-restructuring letters tailored to each borrower's hardship circumstances. How should the analytics lead categorize System X and System Y?
options: Both System X and System Y are generative models because both run on cloud infrastructure.
System X is a generative model creating numerical probabilities, while System Y is a discriminative model filtering grammar.
System X is a discriminative model learning decision boundaries to predict a target label/probability, whereas System Y is a generative model synthesizing novel unstructured text.
Both System X and System Y are unsupervised clustering models because neither uses historical borrower records.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because discriminative models learn the conditional boundary P(Y|X) to classify or score inputs (like predicting default probability from credit features), whereas generative models learn underlying data distributions to produce brand-new outputs (like drafting personalized hardship letters). Option A conflates cloud hosting with model architecture. Option B swaps the definitions of discriminative and generative models. Option D is wrong because default scoring is classic supervised learning using labeled historical outcomes.
questions.use_case: Banks routinely combine a discriminative Vertex AI Tabular / BigQuery ML risk model for precise scoring with a generative Gemini model that translates structured risk decisions into clear customer communications.
questions.hack: Predict a label/score/boundary = Discriminative; Create brand-new text/image/audio/code = Generative.

questions.domain: Domain 3: Techniques to Improve Generative AI Model Output
questions.stem: A regional hospital network is launching a patient-facing appointment and pre-visit preparation chatbot powered by Gemini on Vertex AI. Clinical leadership requires that across every single conversation turn, the assistant must speak at a compassionate sixth-grade reading level, never diagnose medical conditions, and direct emergency symptoms immediately to 911 -- regardless of how patients phrase their questions. Which prompt engineering mechanism is designed specifically to enforce these persistent behavioral boundaries?
options: Repeating the entire policy manually inside every user message after the patient types their question.
Configuring dedicated System Instructions with clear persona, tone, and refusal guardrails separated from untrusted user turns.
Setting Max Output Tokens to 15 so the model cannot write enough words to give medical advice.
Raising Top-K to its maximum value so the model samples more cautious medical vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because System Instructions (combined with role/persona prompting) establish persistent, high-priority behavioral directives -- tone, audience reading level, safety disclaimers, and refusal rules -- in a dedicated system channel separate from user input. Option A is fragile, wastes input tokens redundantly, and mixes policy rules into the untrusted user turn. Option C truncates helpful patient preparation answers without actually governing clinical safety behavior. Option D increases token diversity rather than enforcing clinical refusal policies.
questions.use_case: Healthcare, banking, and HR assistants configure strict Vertex AI System Instructions defining persona, compliance disclaimers, and off-topic refusal behavior alongside Vertex AI safety filters.
questions.hack: Persistent persona, tone, and mandatory refusal rules across all user turns = System Instructions.

questions.domain: Domain 2: Google Cloud's Generative AI Offerings
questions.stem: A Chief Technology Officer is presenting Google Cloud's 5-Layer Generative AI Stack to enterprise architects and must accurately map four concrete organizational initiatives to the corresponding stack layers: (1) Provisioning Cloud TPU Trillium slices for custom foundation training, (2) Governing model registry, evaluation pipelines, and VPC-SC endpoints, (3) Evaluating Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and Llama models from one curated catalog, and (4) Deploying Gemini for Google Workspace and Agentspace for business employees. Which option matches all four initiatives to the correct Google Cloud AI stack layers?
options: 1) Models -> Cloud TPUs | 2) Applications -> Vertex AI | 3) Infrastructure -> Model Garden | 4) Platform -> Gemini for Workspace & Agentspace.
1) Platform -> Cloud TPUs | 2) Infrastructure -> Vertex AI | 3) Agents -> Model Garden | 4) Models -> Gemini for Workspace & Agentspace.
1) Infrastructure -> Cloud TPUs / NVIDIA GPUs | 2) Platform -> Vertex AI | 3) Models -> Model Garden | 4) Applications -> Gemini for Google Workspace & Agentspace.
1) Agents -> Cloud TPUs | 2) Models -> Vertex AI | 3) Applications -> Model Garden | 4) Infrastructure -> Gemini for Google Workspace & Agentspace.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Google Cloud's 5-Layer AI Stack builds cleanly from bottom to top: Layer 1 Infrastructure (Cloud TPUs & NVIDIA GPUs / AI Hypercomputer) -> Layer 2 Platform (Vertex AI unified MLOps/governance) -> Layer 3 Models (Model Garden hosting 1st-party Gemini/Imagen/Veo, partner Claude, and open Llama/Gemma models) -> Layer 4 Applications (ready-to-use Gemini for Workspace, Gemini Code Assist, Agentspace, CES) -> Layer 5 Agents (Vertex AI Agent Builder for autonomous multi-step task execution). Options A, B, and D mismatch hardware, platform, model catalog, and end-user application layers.
questions.use_case: Enterprise architecture review boards use Google Cloud's 5-layer AI stack diagram to decide whether a business need should be satisfied high in the stack (SaaS Applications/Agents) or lower down (custom Platform/Infrastructure).
questions.hack: Google Cloud 5-Layer AI Stack (bottom -> top): Infrastructure (TPUs/GPUs) -> Platform (Vertex AI) -> Models (Model Garden) -> Applications (Workspace/Agentspace/Code Assist) -> Agents (Agent Builder).

questions.domain: Domain 4: Business Strategies for Successful GenAI Solutions
questions.stem: A diversified consumer conglomerate operates 12 regional subsidiaries. Over the past quarter, seven subsidiaries independently evaluated overlapping GenAI tools, hired different consultants to solve identical RAG security challenges, and produced inconsistent Responsible AI review checklists. What governance structure should the Chief Digital Officer establish to scale GenAI safely and efficiently across all 12 business units?
options: Establish a cross-functional AI Center of Excellence (CoE) to define shared security/Responsible AI standards, reusable reference architectures, and enablement playbooks while empowering business units to build domain use cases.
Require all 12 subsidiaries to pause digital transformation for two years while a single isolated R&D lab builds every business app centrally.
Decentralize all vendor contracting and security reviews completely so each team writes its own compliance rules without coordination.
Mandate that only the marketing department may use Generative AI until full ROI is proven across all 12 countries.
questions.explanation: Option A is correct because an AI Center of Excellence (CoE) acts as a cross-functional hub (uniting engineering, security, legal, FinOps, and product leaders) that publishes reusable Vertex AI templates, standardizes Responsible AI and SAIF guardrails, shares lessons learned, and accelerates federated delivery across business units without bottlenecking them. Option B creates a central bottleneck that stalls innovation across the enterprise. Option C perpetuates duplicated spend, inconsistent security, and shadow AI risk. Option D arbitrarily blocks high-ROI use cases in customer service, engineering, and operations.
questions.use_case: Multi-brand enterprises launch a hub-and-spoke AI CoE that maintains pre-approved Vertex AI Terraform landing zones, model-evaluation harnesses, and SAIF security reviews for every subsidiary.
questions.hack: Duplicated vendor evaluations + inconsistent AI security across business units = establish an AI Center of Excellence (CoE).

questions.stem: A B2B software vendor is reviewing how leading foundation models evolve from raw next-token text predictors into helpful, polite, instruction-following enterprise assistants that refuse harmful requests. During an architecture seminar, a manager asks which post-training paradigm uses human preference rankings to train a reward model and iteratively align the LLM's behavior with human expectations. Which technique is being described?
options: Unsupervised k-means clustering over raw web crawls.
Linear regression feature scaling prior to batch inference.
Static stop-sequence truncation during token decoding.
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
questions.explanation: Option D is correct because Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) collects human rankings comparing alternative model responses, trains a reward model capturing human preferences (helpfulness, harmlessness, tone, instruction adherence), and optimizes the LLM policy using reinforcement learning. Option A groups unlabeled data into clusters rather than aligning conversational behavior. Option B is a classical numerical preprocessing step unrelated to LLM alignment. Option C only halts text output when a specific character string appears.
questions.use_case: Model providers and specialized enterprises use RLHF (and variants like RLAIF / DPO) to turn raw pre-trained language models into safe, aligned conversational assistants suitable for customer-facing channels.
questions.hack: Human preference rankings + reward model + aligning helpfulness/safety/tone = RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback).

questions.domain: Domain 2: Google Cloud's Generative AI Offerings
questions.stem: A global e-commerce marketplace receives 15 million customer product reviews and seller messages per day and needs to classify sentiment, extract defective-part mentions, and route urgent safety complaints in under 400 milliseconds per request while keeping inference spend tightly controlled. Which Google Cloud foundation model family tier offers the optimal balance of speed, quality, and token economics?
options: Veo, because high-volume sentiment classification requires temporal video rendering.
Gemini Flash (or Gemini Flash-Lite), engineered for high-throughput, low-latency, cost-efficient multimodal and text workloads at scale.
Pre-training a brand-new 100-billion-parameter model from scratch on Cloud TPUs exclusively for sentiment tagging.
NotebookLM Enterprise, because its Audio Overviews automatically stream 15 million real-time JSON webhooks per day.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct because Gemini Flash and Gemini Flash-Lite are purpose-built for high-frequency, low-latency, cost-sensitive production pipelines such as large-scale classification, extraction, routing, and summarization. Option A (Veo) is a video generation model completely mismatched to text triage. Option C wastes millions in compute and months of R&D on a commodity classification task. Option D (NotebookLM Enterprise) is an interactive research and synthesis application for human knowledge workers, not a high-throughput real-time API.
questions.use_case: High-traffic marketplaces and ad-tech pipelines deploy Gemini Flash / Flash-Lite on Vertex AI for real-time review moderation, intent routing, and structured entity extraction at a fraction of Pro-tier cost.
questions.hack: Millions of daily requests + low latency + tight budget = Gemini Flash / Gemini Flash-Lite.

questions.domain: Domain 3: Techniques to Improve Generative AI Model Output
questions.stem: A corporate tax advisory team uses a Vertex AI Gemini endpoint to calculate multi-jurisdiction depreciation schedules and tiered excise exemptions from client worksheets. When prompted simply with 'Return only the final net tax owed,' the model frequently makes multi-step arithmetic slips. Which prompting technique directly improves accuracy on multi-step logical and mathematical reasoning?
options: Zero-shot single-word prompting with Max Output Tokens capped at 5.
Removing all domain context so the model relies solely on memorized pre-training weights.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, instructing the model to work through intermediate calculation steps explicitly before stating the final result.
Setting Temperature to 1.8 so the model averages random numerical guesses.
questions.explanation: Option C is correct because Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting guides the model to decompose complex reasoning into explicit intermediate steps, allocating computation across sequential reasoning tokens and sharply reducing arithmetic and multi-hop logic errors (and making calculations auditable by tax analysts). Option A forces the model to jump straight to the final number in a single forward pass, causing the exact errors observed. Option B strips necessary client figures from the prompt. Option D introduces extreme randomness, making financial numbers unreliable.
questions.use_case: Finance, insurance underwriting, and supply-chain optimization workflows use Chain-of-Thought prompting (often paired with tool/calculator function calling) to audit step-by-step derivations before recording final outputs.
questions.hack: Multi-step math, logic, or policy deduction errors -> use Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting ('think step by step').

questions.stem: A national telecommunications provider is categorizing its annual Generative AI portfolio using Google Cloud's four core enterprise value pillars: Create, Summarize, Discover, and Automate. The Chief Strategy Officer wants to highlight initiatives that belong specifically to the Discover and Automate pillars during the investor presentation. Which TWO initiatives correctly represent Discover and Automate? (Select TWO.)
options: Discover: Enabling network engineers to search across 12 years of unstructured outage logs, vendor manuals, and schematic PDFs using natural language to pinpoint root causes rapidly.
Automate: Asking a copywriter to brainstorm five new brand slogans for a holiday billboard campaign.
Discover: Condensing a 90-minute quarterly earnings call transcript into a three-paragraph executive memo.
Automate: Deploying an AI agent that validates residential broadband outage alerts, runs diagnostic API checks, opens dispatch tickets, and notifies affected subscribers end-to-end.
Automate: Generating photorealistic product mockups for a print retail brochure.
questions.explanation: Options A and D are correct. Option A exemplifies the Discover pillar by helping employees surface hidden insights and synthesize institutional knowledge across vast unstructured enterprise repositories. Option D exemplifies the Automate pillar by orchestrating multi-step operational workflows and external API actions with minimal manual toil. Options B and E belong to the Create pillar (authoring new marketing copy and visual assets). Option C belongs to the Summarize pillar (distilling long transcripts into concise executive briefs).
questions.use_case: Telecom and enterprise IT leaders map GenAI roadmaps across Create, Summarize, Discover, and Automate to balance quick-win employee productivity (Summarize/Discover) with high-ROI operational workflows (Automate).
questions.hack: 4 Enterprise GenAI Value Pillars: Create (new content), Summarize (condense), Discover (search/insight), Automate (execute multi-step actions).
